People, organisations and run-together names

Source: vignettes/name-types.Rmd
name-types.Rmd

Officer and board lists hold more than people’s names. A bank serves as a foundation’s trustee, a filer writes SEE SCHEDULE O where a name should go, a couple is listed on one line, or a name is typed with no space between the surname and the given name. This article covers two optional tools for these cases:

  • classify_names() labels each entry as a person, an organisation, a person and an organisation, several people, or a placeholder;
  • split_run_together() splits a surname and given name written as one word.

Neither runs unless asked. parse_names() turns them on with classify = TRUE and split_run_together = TRUE.

How common these cases are

Counts on the person-name field of Form 990 Part VII, 2009-2025 (60.8 million rows, 9.5 million distinct names):

Entry Share of rows Examples
A person’s name about 99.5% JOHN A SMITH
A person with a date or note about 0.3% KAREN JONES EXP 2019
An organisation about 0.05% PNC BANK NA, TEAMSTERS LOCAL NO 338
A placeholder about 0.05% SEE SCHEDULE O, VACANT
Several people about 0.02% MICHAEL AND ASHLEY SMITH
A surname and given name run together about 0.01% KramerKenneth, MURPHYSANDRA

The shares are small, but these entries are concentrated: organisations appear again and again (THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON is listed as trustee 939 times), and every one of them, parsed as a person, is a false match waiting to happen.

Classifying names 

x <- c("JOHN A SMITH", "PNC BANK NA", "TEAMSTERS LOCAL NO 338", "BNY MELLON",
       "SEE SCHEDULE O", "VACANT", "MICHAEL AND ASHLEY SMITH",
       "MARY SHURTS - LHS INC", "LARRY CHURCH", "SEE MOUA")
classify_names(x)
#>                        name               name_type org_score
#> 1              JOHN A SMITH                  person    0.0012
#> 2               PNC BANK NA            organisation    0.9999
#> 3    TEAMSTERS LOCAL NO 338            organisation    0.9998
#> 4                BNY MELLON            organisation    0.0412
#> 5            SEE SCHEDULE O             placeholder    0.0074
#> 6                    VACANT             placeholder    0.0193
#> 7  MICHAEL AND ASHLEY SMITH          several people    0.0227
#> 8     MARY SHURTS - LHS INC person and organisation    0.9802
#> 9              LARRY CHURCH                  person    0.0146
#> 10                 SEE MOUA                  person    0.0004
  • Placeholders are found by rules: notes such as SEE SCHEDULE O, NONE, VACANT, NO COMPENSATED OFFICERS, or nothing left after cleaning. SEE followed by a name (SEE MOUA) is a person: SEE is also a given name.
  • Several people are found by AND or & with a given name on at least one side, or by AND in a three-word or longer name that is not an organisation.
  • Organisations are found by a model (next section), plus a short list of institutions that serve as trustees under names with no organisation word, such as BNY MELLON and WELLS FARGO. The list holds names ticked as institutional trustee at five or more organisations, on at least 80% of their organisations and rows.
  • A person and an organisation is an organisation whose first two words are a given name and a surname (MARY SHURTS - LHS INC, an employer after the name). Organisations named after a person (KURT SUZUKI FAMILY FOUNDATION) stay organisations, unless a dash separates the parts.

parse_names(x, classify = TRUE) adds the name_type and org_score columns to the parsed names, so the non-people can be set aside:

p <- parse_names(x, classify = TRUE)
p[, c("name", "first_name", "last_name", "name_type")]
#>                        name first_name last_name               name_type
#> 1              JOHN A SMITH       JOHN     SMITH                  person
#> 2               PNC BANK NA        PNC   BANK-NA            organisation
#> 3    TEAMSTERS LOCAL NO 338  TEAMSTERS  LOCAL-NO            organisation
#> 4                BNY MELLON        BNY    MELLON            organisation
#> 5            SEE SCHEDULE O                                  placeholder
#> 6                    VACANT               VACANT             placeholder
#> 7  MICHAEL AND ASHLEY SMITH    MICHAEL     SMITH          several people
#> 8     MARY SHURTS - LHS INC       MARY    SHURTS person and organisation
#> 9              LARRY CHURCH      LARRY    CHURCH                  person
#> 10                 SEE MOUA        SEE      MOUA                  person

The organisation model

Each word gets a score: the log of how much more often it appears in organisation names than in people’s names. BANK, LODGE and LLC score high; JOHN and SMITH score low. A logistic regression combines the word scores with the number of words, the share of words that are given names or surnames in census.names, and whether the name starts with a given name followed by a surname. org_score is the model’s probability that the name is an organisation.

The model was trained on Form 990 Part VII names, 2009-2025:

  • organisations: 982,000 filers’ own names, plus person-field names with a legal-form word (INC, LLC, BANK) that do not start with a person’s name;
  • people: the other 9.4 million distinct names in the person-name field.

The word scores come from two thirds of the names, and the regression was fit and tested on the rest. On the held-out names (AUC 0.9996):

Words in the name Organisations found People flagged as organisations
1 6% 1.3%
2 77% 0.01%
3 98% 0.10%
4 or more 99% 0.6%

Names of one or two words need org_score of at least 0.99 to count as an organisation, longer names 0.95, because most short entries are people and short organisation names (MUNROE EAGLES) are hard to tell apart from people’s names. Pass threshold = to use one cut-off for all names.

Many of the “people flagged” in the table are not people either: the person-name field also holds unlabelled organisations and notes. In a random sample of flagged names, about one in ten was a person with no organisation in the entry (DAWSON HER MANY HORSES); the rest were organisations, placeholders, or a person with an employer.

The training and test code is in data-raw/name_type_model.R, and the checks in this article in data-raw/name_type_eval.R.

Limits

  • An organisation written as a person’s name (PAULA MILLER for a trust officer, or a small business called by its owner’s name) is a person.
  • Short organisation names without organisation words (CLAY ELEMENTARY, LAZY LADY) are often missed.
  • People whose names are all rare words (DAWSON HER MANY HORSES) can be scored as organisations.
  • A note in the middle of an entry, rather than at the end, can push a person’s name toward organisation.

Splitting run-together names 

split_run_together(c("KramerKenneth", "LedbetterJennifer A", "MURPHYSANDRA",
                     "KLINESUZANNE", "McDonald", "LaToya Jones", "JOHN MARKWALD",
                     "MARKWALD J"))
#> [1] "Kramer Kenneth"       "Ledbetter Jennifer A" "MURPHY SANDRA"        "KLINE SUZANNE"       
#> [5] "McDonald"             "LaToya Jones"         "JOHN MARKWALD"        "MARKWALD J"

A word is split only when the whole word is not a census name and the two parts are a strong surname and a strong given name:

  • With a capital inside the word (KramerKenneth), at the capital. Words that start with a surname particle (McDonald, MacArthur, LaToya, DeShawn, VanDyke) are not split there.
  • In all capitals (MURPHYSANDRA), only when the word is the only word of two or more letters in the name, has eight or more letters, and splits into parts of four or more letters with stricter census evidence. Real surnames that look like two names (MARKWALD, PEARLSTONE) recur across many different names in Form 990 filings, so the 214 such words are never split.

The parser’s order rules then decide which part is the surname:

parse_names(c("LedbetterJennifer A", "KramerKenneth", "MURPHYSANDRA"),
            split_run_together = TRUE)[, c("name", "first_name", "middle_name", "last_name")]
#>                  name first_name middle_name last_name
#> 1 LedbetterJennifer A   JENNIFER           A LEDBETTER
#> 2       KramerKenneth    KENNETH                KRAMER
#> 3        MURPHYSANDRA     SANDRA                MURPHY

On the Part VII names, the capital-letter rule splits 2,014 distinct words (4,524 rows) and the all-capitals rule 1,093 (2,131 rows). In random samples of 40, about 37 and 39 splits were right. The errors are given names or surnames with an inner capital (ChaMira, RiverWind) and rare surnames that are two names (M HEADERICK becomes HEAD ERICK).
